claim: Akt activation in human cancers exerts chemoresistance.
source: Akt activation in human cancers exerts chemoresistance, but pan-Akt inhibition elicits adverse consequences.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract presenting established knowledge about Akt's role in cancer.

claim: Pan-Akt inhibition elicits adverse consequences.
source: Akt activation in human cancers exerts chemoresistance, but pan-Akt inhibition elicits adverse consequences.
evidence: This is a statement in the abstract presenting established knowledge about the side effects of pan-Akt inhibition.

claim: PTEN-deficient prostate cancer cells that display hyperactivated Akt have high intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels.
source: PTEN-deficient prostate cancer cells that display hyperactivated Akt have high intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels, in part, because of Akt-dependent increase of oxidative phosphorylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically in Figure 1D and 1E showing ROS levels in different cell lines.

claim: High intracellular ROS levels in PTEN-deficient prostate cancer cells are in part because of Akt-dependent increase of oxidative phosphorylation.
source: PTEN-deficient prostate cancer cells that display hyperactivated Akt have high intracellular reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels, in part, because of Akt-dependent increase of oxidative phosphorylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing oxygen consumption rates and the effect of Akt knockdown on ROS levels (Figure 1B, 1C, 1F).

claim: High intracellular ROS levels selectively sensitize cells displaying hyperactive Akt to ROS-induced cell death.
source: High intracellular ROS levels selectively sensitize cells displaying hyperactive Akt to ROS-induced cell death enabling a therapeutic strategy combining a ROS inducer and rapamycin in PTEN-deficient prostate tumors in mouse models.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing differential sensitivity of PTEN-deficient vs PTEN-proficient cells to ROS inducers (Figure 2A, 2B).

claim: A therapeutic strategy combining a ROS inducer and rapamycin elicited tumor regression in PTEN-deficient prostate tumors in mouse models.
source: High intracellular ROS levels selectively sensitize cells displaying hyperactive Akt to ROS-induced cell death enabling a therapeutic strategy combining a ROS inducer and rapamycin in PTEN-deficient prostate tumors in mouse models. This strategy elicited tumor regression, and markedly increased survival even after the treatment was stopped.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from xenograft and mouse model studies (Figure 2E, Figure 3, Figure 4).

claim: The combination of ROS inducer and rapamycin markedly increased survival even after the treatment was stopped.
source: This strategy elicited tumor regression, and markedly increased survival even after the treatment was stopped.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data from mouse models (Figure 3G, Figure 4J).

claim: Exposure to antioxidant increased prostate tumor progression.
source: By contrast, exposure to antioxidant increased prostate tumor progression.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing increased prostate weights and tumor grade in NAC-treated mice (Figure 3H, Table 1).

claim: Akt activation phosphorylated HK2 to increase glucose metabolism.
source: To increase glucose metabolism, Akt activation phosphorylated HK2 and induced its expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Miyamoto et al., 2008) and experimental data showing HK2 expression patterns.

claim: Akt activation induced HK2 expression to increase glucose metabolism.
source: To increase glucose metabolism, Akt activation phosphorylated HK2 and induced its expression.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing HK2 expression in PTEN-deficient cells and its dependence on Akt (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 2, Figure 5—figure supplement 3).

claim: HK2 deficiency in mouse models of Pten-deficient prostate cancer elicited a marked inhibition of tumor development.
source: Indeed, HK2 deficiency in mouse models of Pten-deficient prostate cancer elicited a marked inhibition of tumor development and extended lifespan.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Pbsn-Cre4;Ptenf/f;Hk2f/f mice (Figure 6B, 6D, 6E).

claim: HK2 deficiency in mouse models of Pten-deficient prostate cancer extended lifespan.
source: Indeed, HK2 deficiency in mouse models of Pten-deficient prostate cancer elicited a marked inhibition of tumor development and extended lifespan.
evidence: This claim is supported by survival data from Pbsn-Cre4;Ptenf/f;Hk2f/f mice (Figure 6C).

claim: Akt is hyperactivated in cancer by multiple mechanisms, largely through the activation of its upstream regulator phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K).
source: Akt is hyperactivated in cancer by multiple mechanisms, largely through the activation of its upstream regulator phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K), which generates the phosphatidylinositol-3,4,5-trisphophate (PIP3) required for Akt activation (Mayer and Arteaga, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Mayer and Arteaga, 2016.

claim: PI3K generates the phosphatidylinositol-3,4,5-trisphophate (PIP3) required for Akt activation.
source: Akt is hyperactivated in cancer by multiple mechanisms, largely through the activation of its upstream regulator phosphoinositide 3-kinase (PI3K), which generates the phosphatidylinositol-3,4,5-trisphophate (PIP3) required for Akt activation (Mayer and Arteaga, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Mayer and Arteaga, 2016 and represents established knowledge.

claim: The activity of PI3K is negatively regulated by the tumor suppressor Phosphatase And Tensin Homolog (PTEN).
source: The activity of PI3K is negatively regulated by the tumor suppressor Phosphatase And Tensin Homolog (PTEN), which is a PIP3 phosphatase, and therefore inhibits the PI3K/Akt signaling pathway.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about the PI3K/Akt pathway.

claim: PTEN is a PIP3 phosphatase.
source: The activity of PI3K is negatively regulated by the tumor suppressor Phosphatase And Tensin Homolog (PTEN), which is a PIP3 phosphatase, and therefore inhibits the PI3K/Akt signaling pathway.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about PTEN function.

claim: PTEN inhibits the PI3K/Akt signaling pathway.
source: The activity of PI3K is negatively regulated by the tumor suppressor Phosphatase And Tensin Homolog (PTEN), which is a PIP3 phosphatase, and therefore inhibits the PI3K/Akt signaling pathway.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about PTEN function.

claim: PTEN expression is often lost in human cancers, specifically in glioblastoma, melanoma, endometrial, and prostate cancers.
source: PTEN expression is often lost in human cancers, specifically in glioblastoma, melanoma, endometrial, and prostate cancers (Hollander et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hollander et al., 2011.

claim: The activation of PI3K/Akt signaling in cancer and its ability to exert chemoresistance led to the development of small molecule inhibitors of PI3K and Akt.
source: The activation of PI3K/Akt signaling in cancer and its ability to exert chemoresistance led to the development of small molecule inhibitors of PI3K and Akt, which are currently being tested in clinical trials (Kim et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2017; Zheng, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kim et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2017; Zheng, 2017.

claim: Small molecule inhibitors of PI3K and Akt are currently being tested in clinical trials.
source: The activation of PI3K/Akt signaling in cancer and its ability to exert chemoresistance led to the development of small molecule inhibitors of PI3K and Akt, which are currently being tested in clinical trials (Kim et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2017; Zheng, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kim et al., 2005; Zhang et al., 2017; Zheng, 2017.

claim: There are three Akt genes in mammalian cells (Akt1-3).
source: There are three Akt genes in mammalian cells (Akt1-3), and their encoded proteins have a high degree of identical amino acids; however, the expression pattern in mammalian tissues and organs is different among the three isoforms.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about Akt isoforms.

claim: The three Akt proteins have a high degree of identical amino acids.
source: There are three Akt genes in mammalian cells (Akt1-3), and their encoded proteins have a high degree of identical amino acids; however, the expression pattern in mammalian tissues and organs is different among the three isoforms.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about Akt isoforms.

claim: The expression pattern in mammalian tissues and organs is different among the three Akt isoforms.
source: There are three Akt genes in mammalian cells (Akt1-3), and their encoded proteins have a high degree of identical amino acids; however, the expression pattern in mammalian tissues and organs is different among the three isoforms.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about Akt isoforms.

claim: Akt1 is ubiquitously expressed.
source: While Akt1 is ubiquitously expressed, Akt2 is expressed at the highest level in insulin-responsive tissues, and Akt3 is expressed at the highest level in the brain.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about Akt1 expression.

claim: Akt2 is expressed at the highest level in insulin-responsive tissues.
source: While Akt1 is ubiquitously expressed, Akt2 is expressed at the highest level in insulin-responsive tissues, and Akt3 is expressed at the highest level in the brain.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about Akt2 expression.

claim: Akt3 is expressed at the highest level in the brain.
source: While Akt1 is ubiquitously expressed, Akt2 is expressed at the highest level in insulin-responsive tissues, and Akt3 is expressed at the highest level in the brain.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about Akt3 expression.

claim: Different mouse phenotypes with individual Akt isoform germ line deletions can be explained by their relative expression in the organs that determine the phenotype.
source: Different mouse phenotypes with individual Akt isoform germ line deletions can be explained by their relative expression in the organs that determine the phenotype (Dummler and Hemmings, 2007; Hay, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dummler and Hemmings, 2007; Hay, 2011.

claim: The Akt inhibitors currently in clinical trials are pan-Akt inhibitors that inhibit the different Akt isoforms to a similar extent.
source: The Akt inhibitors currently in clinical trials are pan-Akt inhibitors that inhibit the different Akt isoforms to a similar extent; however, these pan-Akt inhibitors exert undesired side effects, such as hyperglycemia, hyperinsulinemia, and diabetes (Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2017.

claim: Pan-Akt inhibitors exert undesired side effects, such as hyperglycemia, hyperinsulinemia, and diabetes.
source: The Akt inhibitors currently in clinical trials are pan-Akt inhibitors that inhibit the different Akt isoforms to a similar extent; however, these pan-Akt inhibitors exert undesired side effects, such as hyperglycemia, hyperinsulinemia, and diabetes (Wang et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2017.

claim: Genetic deletion of Akt1 and Akt2 in the mouse liver induces liver damage, inflammation, and paradoxically hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC).
source: Furthermore, genetic deletion of Akt1 and Akt2 in the mouse liver induces liver damage, inflammation, and paradoxically hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) (Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2016.

claim: The most evolutionarily conserved function of Akt is mediating cellular and organismal metabolism.
source: Perhaps the most evolutionarily conserved function of Akt is mediating cellular and organismal metabolism.
evidence: This represents established knowledge about Akt function.

claim: PTEN is lost in approximately 40% of prostate cancers.
source: As PTEN is lost in approximately 40% of prostate cancers (Pourmand et al., 2007; Taylor et al., 2010), we chose to work towards developing a personalized therapeutic approach using PTEN-deficient prostate cancer to explore selective vulnerability as a consequence of Akt's metabolic activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Pourmand et al., 2007; Taylor et al., 2010.

claim: Activation of Akt increases both glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation.
source: As we showed previously, activation of Akt increases both glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation (Gottlob et al., 2001; Robey and Hay, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gottlob et al., 2001; Robey and Hay, 2009.

claim: Akt activation increases intracellular ROS levels, in part by increasing oxidative phosphorylation.
source: We also showed that Akt activation increases intracellular ROS levels, in part by increasing oxidative phosphorylation.
evidence: This claim is supported by previous work and data in the manuscript (Figure 1).

claim: Akt does not exert resistance to ROS-induced cell death.
source: As Akt does not exert resistance to ROS-induced cell death, increasing ROS levels could selectively eradicate cells displaying hyperactive Akt (Nogueira et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Nogueira et al., 2008 and data in Figure 2.

claim: Human PTEN-deficient prostate cancer cells have high intracellular ROS levels, which are Akt-dependent.
source: Here, we showed that human PTEN-deficient and not PTEN-proficient prostate cancer cells have high intracellular ROS levels, which are Akt-dependent.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 1D, 1E, 1F.

claim: Human PTEN-proficient prostate cancer cells do not have high intracellular ROS levels.
source: Here, we showed that human PTEN-deficient and not PTEN-proficient prostate cancer cells have high intracellular ROS levels, which are Akt-dependent.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 1D, 1E showing lower ROS levels in DU145 cells.

claim: Phenylethyl isothiocyanate (PEITC) depletes intracellular glutathione.
source: We used the natural compound phenylethyl isothiocyanate (PEITC), which depletes intracellular glutathione (Xu and Thornalley, 2001), as a ROS inducer either alone or in combination with the mTORC1 inhibitor rapamycin to selectively eradicate Pten-deficient cancer cells in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Xu and Thornalley, 2001 and data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: In PTEN-deficient prostate cancer, HK2 is induced because of Akt activation to increase glycolysis.
source: We also found that in PTEN-deficient prostate cancer, HK2 is induced because of Akt activation to increase glycolysis.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 5A and supplementary figures.

claim: HK2 is the hexokinase isoform that is not highly expressed in most mammalian tissues but is generally induced in cancer cells by multiple mechanisms.
source: HK2 is the hexokinase isoform that is not highly expressed in most mammalian tissues but is generally induced in cancer cells by multiple mechanisms (Hay, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hay, 2016.

claim: HK2 is phosphorylated by Akt to increase its mitochondrial binding.
source: Furthermore, HK2 is phosphorylated by Akt to increase its mitochondrial binding (Miyamoto et al., 2008) and therefore its glycolytic activity (DeWaal et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Miyamoto et al., 2008.

claim: HK2 mitochondrial binding increases its glycolytic activity.
source: Furthermore, HK2 is phosphorylated by Akt to increase its mitochondrial binding (Miyamoto et al., 2008) and therefore its glycolytic activity (DeWaal et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to DeWaal et al., 2018.

claim: Silencing HK2 in human PTEN-deficient prostate tumors inhibits cancer development in both cytostatic and cytotoxic manners.
source: Here we show that silencing HK2 in human PTEN-deficient prostate tumors and deleting HK2 in a mouse model of Pten-deficient prostate cancer inhibits cancer development in both cytostatic and cytotoxic manners.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 5H and Figure 5—figure supplement 7.

claim: Deleting HK2 in a mouse model of Pten-deficient prostate cancer inhibits cancer development in both cytostatic and cytotoxic manners.
source: Here we show that silencing HK2 in human PTEN-deficient prostate tumors and deleting HK2 in a mouse model of Pten-deficient prostate cancer inhibits cancer development in both cytostatic and cytotoxic manners.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 6D, 6E.

claim: HK2 deficiency overcomes the chemoresistance of PTEN-deficient prostate cancer cells.
source: HK2 deficiency also overcomes the chemoresistance of PTEN-deficient prostate cancer cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 5G, 5H.

claim: DU145 cells harbor wild-type PTEN and exhibit low Akt activity.
source: DU145 cells, which harbor wild-type PTEN, exhibit low Akt activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 1A.

claim: PTEN-deficient PC3 and LNCaP cells display hyperactivated Akt.
source: PTEN-deficient PC3 and LNCaP cells display hyperactivated Akt.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 1A.

claim: Akt elevates oxygen consumption.
source: As we previously found, Akt elevates oxygen consumption and intracellular ROS levels (Nogueira et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Nogueira et al., 2008 and data in Figure 1B, 1C.

claim: Basal oxygen consumption was lowest in the PTEN-proficient DU145 cells.
source: Basal oxygen consumption was lowest in the PTEN-proficient DU145 cells, while it was gradually increased in the PTEN-deficient PC3 and LNCaP cells (Figure 1B), following the pattern of Akt activity in which higher oxygen consumption was correlated with higher Akt activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Basal oxygen consumption was gradually increased in the PTEN-deficient PC3 and LNCaP cells.
source: Basal oxygen consumption was lowest in the PTEN-proficient DU145 cells, while it was gradually increased in the PTEN-deficient PC3 and LNCaP cells (Figure 1B), following the pattern of Akt activity in which higher oxygen consumption was correlated with higher Akt activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Higher oxygen consumption was correlated with higher Akt activity.
source: Basal oxygen consumption was lowest in the PTEN-proficient DU145 cells, while it was gradually increased in the PTEN-deficient PC3 and LNCaP cells (Figure 1B), following the pattern of Akt activity in which higher oxygen consumption was correlated with higher Akt activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and 1B.

claim: Silencing Akt1 and Akt2 in PC3 cells markedly decreased oxygen consumption.
source: Silencing Akt1 and Akt2 in PC3 cells markedly decreased oxygen consumption, indicating that the high oxygen consumption in these cells is Akt-dependent (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The high oxygen consumption in PC3 cells is Akt-dependent.
source: Silencing Akt1 and Akt2 in PC3 cells markedly decreased oxygen consumption, indicating that the high oxygen consumption in these cells is Akt-dependent (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Basal oxygen consumption in DU145 cells reached the maximum capacity of the respiratory chain.
source: Interestingly, basal oxygen consumption in DU145 cells reached the maximum capacity of the respiratory chain, while PC3 and LNCaP cells had a larger spare capacity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: PC3 and LNCaP cells had a larger spare respiratory capacity than DU145 cells.
source: Interestingly, basal oxygen consumption in DU145 cells reached the maximum capacity of the respiratory chain, while PC3 and LNCaP cells had a larger spare capacity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The ATP production capacity is two-fold higher in PC3 and LNCaP cells compared with DU145 cells.
source: Figure 1B also shows that the ATP production capacity is two-fold higher in PC3 and LNCaP cells compared with DU145 cells, agreeing with our previous observations that Akt activation increases ATP production by both glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation (Gottlob et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and citation to Gottlob et al., 2001.

claim: Akt activation increases ATP production by both glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation.
source: Figure 1B also shows that the ATP production capacity is two-fold higher in PC3 and LNCaP cells compared with DU145 cells, agreeing with our previous observations that Akt activation increases ATP production by both glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation (Gottlob et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gottlob et al., 2001.

claim: High Akt activity was correlated with high intracellular levels of ROS.
source: As intracellular ROS are by-products of high OXPHO, we determined intracellular ROS production at the cytosolic (Figure 1D) and mitochondrial (Figure 1E) levels, and found that high Akt activity was correlated with high intracellular levels of ROS.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and 1E.

claim: Akt1 and Akt2 knockdown in PC3 cells decreased ROS levels.
source: Akt1 and Akt2 knockdown in PC3 cells consistently decreased ROS levels, confirming that Akt regulates intracellular ROS levels. (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Akt regulates intracellular ROS levels.
source: Akt1 and Akt2 knockdown in PC3 cells consistently decreased ROS levels, confirming that Akt regulates intracellular ROS levels. (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: In PC3 and LNCaP cells, mitochondrial membrane potential is higher than in DU145 cells.
source: Finally, we found that in PC3 and LNCaP cells, mitochondrial membrane potential is higher than in DU145 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), which is likely correlated with the higher respiratory chain activity in PC3 and LNCaP cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Higher mitochondrial membrane potential in PC3 and LNCaP cells is likely correlated with the higher respiratory chain activity in these cells.
source: Finally, we found that in PC3 and LNCaP cells, mitochondrial membrane potential is higher than in DU145 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), which is likely correlated with the higher respiratory chain activity in PC3 and LNCaP cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data showing both higher mitochondrial membrane potential and higher respiratory chain activity.

claim: Akt activation increases ROS not only by increasing oxygen consumption but also by inhibiting the expression of ROS scavengers downstream of FOXO.
source: In our previous studies, we found that Akt activation increases ROS not only by increasing oxygen consumption but also by inhibiting the expression of ROS scavengers downstream of FOXO, such as MnSOD and catalase, and particularly sestrin3 (Sesn3) (Nogueira et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Nogueira et al., 2008.

claim: Sesn3 is a transcriptional target of FOXO.
source: Sesn3 is a transcriptional target of FOXO (Chen et al., 2010) and a member of a protein family including Sesn1 and Sesn2, which reduce ROS by several mechanisms (Bae et al., 2013; Kopnin et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2010.

claim: Sesn3 is a member of a protein family including Sesn1 and Sesn2, which reduce ROS by several mechanisms.
source: Sesn3 is a transcriptional target of FOXO (Chen et al., 2010) and a member of a protein family including Sesn1 and Sesn2, which reduce ROS by several mechanisms (Bae et al., 2013; Kopnin et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bae et al., 2013; Kopnin et al., 2007.

claim: Changes in MnSOD and catalase expression in the CaP cells did not correlate with changes in ROS levels.
source: Interestingly, in contrast to our findings in MEFs (Nogueira et al., 2008), changes in MnSOD and catalase expression in the CaP cells did not correlate with changes in ROS levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), which is consistent with previously observations (Chowdhury et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and citation to Chowdhury et al., 2007.

claim: The pattern of Sesn3 expression was consistent with ROS levels in CaP cells.
source: However, the pattern of Sesn3 expression was consistent with ROS levels, and while DU145 cells express high levels of Sesn3, PC3 and LNCaP cells express relatively low levels of Sesn3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: DU145 cells express high levels of Sesn3.
source: However, the pattern of Sesn3 expression was consistent with ROS levels, and while DU145 cells express high levels of Sesn3, PC3 and LNCaP cells express relatively low levels of Sesn3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: PC3 and LNCaP cells express relatively low levels of Sesn3.
source: However, the pattern of Sesn3 expression was consistent with ROS levels, and while DU145 cells express high levels of Sesn3, PC3 and LNCaP cells express relatively low levels of Sesn3 (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Downregulation of Sesn3 in DU145 cells was sufficient to increase cytosolic ROS production.
source: Interestingly, downregulation of Sesn3 in DU145 cells or up-regulation of Sesn3 in PC3 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 4) was sufficient to modulate cytosolic ROS production in these cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 5). Sesn3 knockdown in DU145 cells increased ROS production, while overexpression of Sesn3 in PC3 cells decreased ROS production.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4 and Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: Up-regulation of Sesn3 in PC3 cells was sufficient to decrease cytosolic ROS production.
source: Interestingly, downregulation of Sesn3 in DU145 cells or up-regulation of Sesn3 in PC3 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 4) was sufficient to modulate cytosolic ROS production in these cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 5). Sesn3 knockdown in DU145 cells increased ROS production, while overexpression of Sesn3 in PC3 cells decreased ROS production.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4 and Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claim: Sesn3 contributes to the regulation of intracellular ROS downstream of Akt and FoxOs in CaP cells.
source: These results suggest that Sesn3 contributes to the regulation of intracellular ROS downstream of Akt and FoxOs in CaP cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data showing Sesn3's effect on ROS levels.

claim: PTEN-deficient prostate cancer cells display high OXPHO and ROS levels in an Akt-dependent manner.
source: Taken together, these results show that PTEN-deficient prostate cancer cells display high OXPHO and ROS levels in an Akt-dependent manner.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Cells that display high Akt activity could be selectivity killed by increasing the intracellular level of ROS.
source: We previously reported that cells that display high Akt activity could be selectivity killed by increasing the intracellular level of ROS (Nogueira et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Nogueira et al., 2008.

claim: The selectivity of ROS-induced killing results from the high intracellular ROS levels exerted by Akt activation in combination with the inability of Akt to protect against ROS-induced cell death.
source: This selectivity results from the high intracellular ROS levels exerted by Akt activation in combination with the inability of Akt to protect against ROS-induced cell death.
evidence: This is an explanation based on previous findings and current data.

claim: 2-methoxyestradiol (2-ME) is an endogenous metabolite of estradiol-17β that increases ROS.
source: We therefore treated the prostate cancer cells with 2-methoxyestradiol (2-ME), an endogenous metabolite of estradiol-17β that increases ROS, or with β-phenylethyl isothiocyanate (PEITC), a natural compound found in consumable cruciferous vegetables that is known to increase intracellular ROS levels by depleting intracellular glutathione (Ting et al., 2010; Yu et al., 1998; see also Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This represents established knowledge about 2-ME.

claim: PEITC is a natural compound found in consumable cruciferous vegetables.
source: We therefore treated the prostate cancer cells with 2-methoxyestradiol (2-ME), an endogenous metabolite of estradiol-17β that increases ROS, or with β-phenylethyl isothiocyanate (PEITC), a natural compound found in consumable cruciferous vegetables that is known to increase intracellular ROS levels by depleting intracellular glutathione (Ting et al., 2010; Yu et al., 1998; see also Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This represents established knowledge about PEITC.

claim: PEITC is known to increase intracellular ROS levels by depleting intracellular glutathione.
source: We therefore treated the prostate cancer cells with 2-methoxyestradiol (2-ME), an endogenous metabolite of estradiol-17β that increases ROS, or with β-phenylethyl isothiocyanate (PEITC), a natural compound found in consumable cruciferous vegetables that is known to increase intracellular ROS levels by depleting intracellular glutathione (Ting et al., 2010; Yu et al., 1998; see also Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ting et al., 2010; Yu et al., 1998 and data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: CaP cells with high Akt activity resulting from the loss of PTEN (LNCaP, PC3 cells) were more vulnerable to 2-ME- and PEITC-induced cell death than PTEN-proficient CaP cells (DU145 cells).
source: We found that CaP cells with high Akt activity resulting from the loss of PTEN (LNCaP, PC3 cells) were more vulnerable to 2-ME- and PEITC-induced cell death than PTEN-proficient CaP cells (DU145 cells) (Figure 2A,B, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A, 2B, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: LNCaP and PC3 cells are more vulnerable to the glutathione reducing agent BSO.
source: LNCaP and PC3 cells are more vulnerable to the glutathione reducing agent BSO (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: The NADP+/NADPH ratio is elevated in the PTEN-deficient cells.
source: Interestingly, the NADP+/NADPH ratio is elevated in the PTEN-deficient cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: The elevated NADP+/NADPH ratio could be contributing to the high level of ROS in PTEN-deficient cells.
source: The elevated NADP+/NADPH could be either contributing to the high level of ROS or it is a result of increased NADPH consumption to combat the high ROS level.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism.

claim: The elevated NADP+/NADPH ratio could be a result of increased NADPH consumption to combat the high ROS level in PTEN-deficient cells.
source: The elevated NADP+/NADPH could be either contributing to the high level of ROS or it is a result of increased NADPH consumption to combat the high ROS level.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism.

claim: An increase in NADPH consumption for fatty acid synthesis in the PTEN-deficient cells can contribute to the higher NADP+/NADPH ratio.
source: Alternatively or additionally, an increase in NADPH consumption for fatty acid synthesis in the PTEN-deficient cells can contribute to the higher NADP+/NADPH ratio.
evidence: This is speculation about an alternative mechanism.

claim: Silencing Sesn3 increased PEITC-induced cell death in DU145 cells.
source: Silencing Sesn3 increased PEITC-induced cell death in DU145 cells, and overexpression of SESN3in PC3 cells decreased their sensitivity to PEITC (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: Overexpression of SESN3 in PC3 cells decreased their sensitivity to PEITC.
source: Silencing Sesn3 increased PEITC-induced cell death in DU145 cells, and overexpression of SESN3in PC3 cells decreased their sensitivity to PEITC (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: The cell death induced by PEITC is ROS-dependent as it is inhibited by the ROS scavenger N-acetyl cysteine (NAC).
source: The cell death induced by PEITC is ROS-dependent as it is inhibited by the ROS scavenger N-acetyl cysteine (NAC) (Figure 2—figure supplement 6).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 6.

claim: Oxygen consumption and ROS production were increased by silencing Pten in DU145 cells.
source: Oxygen consumption and ROS production were increased by silencing Pten in DU145 cells and decreased in PC3 and LNCaP cells expressing PTEN (Figure 2—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 8.

claim: Oxygen consumption and ROS production were decreased in PC3 and LNCaP cells expressing PTEN.
source: Oxygen consumption and ROS production were increased by silencing Pten in DU145 cells and decreased in PC3 and LNCaP cells expressing PTEN (Figure 2—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 8.

claim: The silencing of Pten in DU145 cells increased sensitivity to PEITC.
source: The silencing of Pten in DU145 cells increased sensitivity to PEITC, whereas the expression of PTEN in PC3 and LNCaP cells decreased their sensitivity to PEITC (Figure 2—figure supplement 9).
